claim: Immunoglobulins (Igs) can specifically recognize a vast variety of natural and man-made organic molecules through recombination and mutation of small numbers of genes.
source: Through recombination and mutation of small numbers of genes, Igs can specifically recognize a vast variety of natural and man-made organic molecules.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about immunoglobulin function and diversity generation.

claim: Jawless vertebrates evolved a parallel system of humoral immunity that recognizes antigens with variable lymphocyte receptor B (VLRB) rather than Ig.
source: Jawless vertebrates evolved a parallel system of humoral immunity, which recognizes antigens not with Ig, but with a structurally unrelated receptor called the variable lymphocyte receptor B (VLRB).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research on jawless vertebrate immunity.

claim: Lamprey VLRB and mouse Ig responses to influenza A virus focus approximately 80% of the response on hemagglutinin (HA).
source: Surprisingly, we find lamprey VLRB and mouse Ig responses to influenza A virus are extremely similar. Each focuses ∼80% of the response on hemagglutinin (HA), mainly through recognition of the major antigenic sites in the HA globular head domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3B.

claim: Lamprey VLRB and mouse Ig responses to influenza A virus mainly recognize the major antigenic sites in the HA globular head domain.
source: Each focuses ∼80% of the response on hemagglutinin (HA), mainly through recognition of the major antigenic sites in the HA globular head domain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from competition assays and binding to mutant viruses shown in Table 1 and Table 2.

claim: Cyclostomes (lampreys and hagfish) are the only known living jawless vertebrates.
source: We characterized the variable lymphocyte receptor B (VLRB) response of lampreys, which along with hagfish, are the only known living jawless vertebrates (cyclostomes).
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Cyclostomes branched evolutionarily from jawed vertebrates approximately 550 million years ago.
source: Cyclostomes branched evolutionarily from jawed vertebrates approximately 550 million years ago (Mya) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by evolutionary biology literature and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Lampreys generate antibody responses to protein and carbohydrate immunogens.
source: Pioneering studies from the Good laboratory established that lampreys generate Ab responses to protein and carbohydrate immunogens (Finstad and Good, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Lamprey VLRBs bear no relationship to Igs but are structurally similar to Toll-like receptors.
source: More than 40 years later, Cooper and colleagues discovered that lamprey Abs, VLRBs, bear no relationship to Igs, but rather are structurally similar to Toll-like receptors (Pancer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: VLRB diversity is generated using a gene assembly mechanism reminiscent of activation-induced cytidine deaminase-catalyzed gene conversion.
source: In place of RAG-mediated V(D)J recombination, VLRB diversity is generated using a gene assembly mechanism reminiscent of the activation-induced cytidine deamine-catalyzed gene conversion mechanism used to diversify Ig genes in birds and some mammals (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The germline VLRB gene is incomplete because the invariant 5′ and 3′ coding sequences are separated by non-coding intervening sequences.
source: The germline VLRB gene is incomplete because the invariant 5′ and 3′ coding sequences are separated by non-coding intervening sequences (Pancer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Several of the hundreds of leucine rich repeat (LRR)-encoding genes flanking the VRLB gene are copied into the gene to generate an in-frame, functional VLRB gene during lymphocyte development.
source: Several of the hundreds of leucine rich repeat (LRR)-encoding genes flanking the VRLB gene are copied into the gene to generate an in-frame, functional VLRB gene during lymphocyte development (Nagawa et al., 2007; Rogozin et al., 2007; Alder et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: VLRB repertoire diversity is comparable to Igs.
source: This generates a VLRB repertoire with diversity comparable to Igs (Alder et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: VLRB encodes single-chain, crescent-shaped proteins that bind to antigens with a concave surface composed of multiple LRR β-strands and a C-terminal variable loop (LRRCT).
source: VLRB encodes for single-chain, crescent-shaped proteins that bind to antigens with a concave surface composed of multiple LRR β-strands and a C-terminal variable loop (LRRCT) (Kim et al., 2007; Han et al., 2008; Herrin et al., 2008; Velikovsky et al., 2009; Kirchdoerfer et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Igs consist of a heavy and a light chain, each of which contributes three complementarity determining region loops to form the antigen-binding site.
source: In contrast, Igs consist of a heavy and a light chain, each of which contributes three complementarity determining region loops to form a structurally distinct antigen-binding site (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about immunoglobulin structure, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Polyclonal VLRB primarily migrates on an SDS-PAGE gel as disulfide-linked multimers under non-reducing conditions and as monomers in the presence of reducing agents.
source: Polyclonal VLRB primarily migrates on an SDS-PAGE gel as disulfide-linked multimers under non-reducing conditions and as monomers in the presence of reducing agents (Alder et al., 2008; Herrin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed by data in Figure 2A.

claim: VLRB levels increase approximately sevenfold after immunization in lampreys.
source: As seen previously (Alder et al., 2005), monitoring plasma VLRB by immunoblotting revealed that unlike mammalian Ig, where immunization induces only minor increases in substantial serum levels, VLRB levels increase ∼sevenfold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to prior research.

claim: Unlike mammalian Ig, where immunization induces only minor increases in substantial serum levels, lamprey VLRB levels increase substantially after immunization.
source: As seen previously (Alder et al., 2005), monitoring plasma VLRB by immunoblotting revealed that unlike mammalian Ig, where immunization induces only minor increases in substantial serum levels, VLRB levels increase ∼sevenfold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and comparison with mammalian Ig responses.

claim: Each immunized lamprey generated VLRBs that bind PR8 but not parainfluenza-3 virus.
source: ELISAs revealed that each immunized lamprey generated VLRBs that bind PR8, but not a similar amount of plate-bound parainfluenza-3 virus, which is a genetically and serologically completely distinct enveloped virus, but similar in architecture and complexity to IAV (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In both mice and lamprey, more than 90% of the functional ELISA response to IAV is specific for HA and NA.
source: This revealed that in both mice and lamprey, more than 90% of the functional ELISA response is specific for HA and NA, as shown by the large difference in titers between detergent soluble proteins from PR8 (H1N1) vs X31 (H3N2), a reassortant virus with the PR8 internal proteins but serologically distinct HK68 glycoproteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upwards of 80% of ELISA-detected antibodies to IAV are specific for HA in lamprey and mice.
source: Genetically isolating HA from NA using the J1 (H3N1, PR8 internal proteins) and P50 (H1N2, HK internal proteins) reassortants shows that upwards of 80% of ELISA-detected Abs are specific for HA in lamprey and mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ELISA data using reassortant viruses shown in Figure 3B.

claim: M1 is negligibly immunogenic in lamprey and mice immunized with IAV.
source: Low binding to X31 and HK soluble proteins, which contain significant amounts of M1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicate that M1 is negligibly immunogenic (note that internal viral proteins from H3 and H1 viruses are antigenically highly conserved).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental ELISA data and Western blot data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only a small fraction of Igs are specific for NP or a low abundance internal virion component.
source: Further, the low serum titers against PR8 cores confirm that only a small fraction of Igs are specific for NP or a low abundance internal virion component.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental ELISA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PR8-immunized lamprey plasma gave HI titers of 1:30 against PR8, but <1:5 against an H3N2 IAV and B/Lee.
source: HI measures the ability of Abs to block HA-mediated IAV attachment to erythrocyte surface terminal sialic acids. PR8-immunized lamprey plasma gave HI titers of 1:30 against PR8, but <1:5 against an H3N2 IAV and B/Lee, an influenza B virus, which is serologically totally distinct from IAV (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental hemagglutination inhibition data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Immune lamprey plasma significantly inhibited PR8 infectivity in MDCK cells relative to naïve plasma.
source: Immune lamprey plasma also significantly inhibited PR8 infectivity in MDCK cells relative to naïve plasma (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental neutralization assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The vast majority of Igs that inhibit IAV hemagglutination and viral infectivity bind the HA globular domain.
source: The vast majority of Igs that inhibit IAV hemagglutination and viral infectivity bind the HA globular domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior influenza research.

claim: Lamprey plasma shows a significant loss of binding to PR8 viruses with six amino acid substitutions in the HA globular domain and a loss of approximately 60% of binding with 12 substitutions.
source: ELISAs using intact wild-type or mutant viruses as immunoadsorbents show that lamprey plasma similarly detect antigenic drift in the globular domain, with a significant loss of binding with six substitutions and a loss of ∼60% of binding with 12 substitutions (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Table 1.

claim: Similar binding patterns to drifted viruses are seen with mouse, guinea pig, and chicken PR8 immune sera.
source: Similar binding is seen with mouse, guinea pig, and chicken PR8 immune seras (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Table 1—source data 1.

claim: The bulk of mouse, guinea pig, chicken and lamprey HA-specific Ig and VLRB recognize the globular head domain.
source: Factoring in the contribution of anti-NA Abs to the signal, this indicates that the bulk of mouse, guinea pig, chicken and lamprey HA-specific Ig and VLRB recognize the globular head domain, and therefore that the globular domain is the immunodominant antigen for both mice and lamprey.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental ELISA data with drifted viruses shown in Table 1.

claim: The globular domain is the immunodominant antigen for both mice and lamprey.
source: Factoring in the contribution of anti-NA Abs to the signal, this indicates that the bulk of mouse, guinea pig, chicken and lamprey HA-specific Ig and VLRB recognize the globular head domain, and therefore that the globular domain is the immunodominant antigen for both mice and lamprey.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental ELISA data shown in Table 1.

claim: Anti-PR8 VLRBs can distinguish antigenic drift in H1N1 isolates from the 1940s and 1950s.
source: As predicted, anti-PR8 VLRBs could easily distinguish antigenic drift in H1N1 isolates from the 1940s and 1950s (Table 1 and Table 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Table 1 and Table 1—source data 2.

claim: Anti-PR8 plasma from lampreys 7 and 9 competed with mouse monoclonal antibodies specific for defined HA antigenic sites.
source: Anti-PR8 plasma from lampreys 7 and 9 (L7, L9) competed with the mAbs tested, whereas neither naïve lamprey plasma nor mAbs to an irrelevant antigen competed with the mAbs (Table 2 and Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental competition ELISA data shown in Table 2.

claim: L9 plasma competes with mAbs specific for each of the five antigenic sites, but L7 fails to compete with Sa and Sb mAbs.
source: Also, while both L7 and L9 have a similar ELISA titer to whole virus, L9 plasma competes with mAbs specific for each of the five sites, but L7 fails to compete with Sa and Sb mAbs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental competition ELISA data shown in Table 2.

claim: VLRB binding to the HA head does not uniformly block binding of all head-specific Igs.
source: This demonstrates that VLRB binding to the HA head does not uniformly block binding of all head-specific Igs and, importantly, indicates that fine antigen specificity varies among individual lampreys.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential competition patterns observed in Table 2.

claim: Fine antigen specificity varies among individual lampreys.
source: This demonstrates that VLRB binding to the HA head does not uniformly block binding of all head-specific Igs and, importantly, indicates that fine antigen specificity varies among individual lampreys.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential competition patterns observed in Table 2.

claim: L29 plasma effectively blocked each of the four Fabs tested.
source: Plasma from an additional lamprey (L29) also effectively blocked each of the four Fabs tested (Table 2 and Table 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental competition ELISA data shown in Table 2 and Table 2—source data 2.

claim: L29 plasma did not block binding of either a representative mouse or human mAb specific for the stem region with broadly neutralizing activity.
source: L29 plasma did not, however, block binding of either a representative mouse or human mAb specific for the stem region with broadly neutralizing activity, suggesting that, as in mammals, the stem region is poorly immunogenic in lampreys (Table 2 and Table 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental competition ELISA data shown in Table 2 and Table 2—source data 3.

claim: The stem region is poorly immunogenic in lampreys, as in mammals.
source: L29 plasma did not, however, block binding of either a representative mouse or human mAb specific for the stem region with broadly neutralizing activity, suggesting that, as in mammals, the stem region is poorly immunogenic in lampreys (Table 2 and Table 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of competition with stem-specific antibodies shown in Table 2—source data 3.

claim: The lamprey immune system focuses on the globular domain, as in man and mouse.
source: Rather, as in man and mouse, the lamprey immune system focuses on the globular domain, and further, recognizes highly similar epitopes.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition data and binding patterns shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Lamprey immune system recognizes highly similar epitopes to man and mouse.
source: Rather, as in man and mouse, the lamprey immune system focuses on the globular domain, and further, recognizes highly similar epitopes.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition data shown in Table 2.

claim: Ig and VLRB demonstrate similar specificity for HA head epitopes.
source: Our findings support the conclusion that Ig and VLRB demonstrate similar specificity for HA head epitopes.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The common effect of amino acid substitution on VLRB and Ig binding argues strongly for convergent recognition of highly overlapping epitopes.
source: Although steric issues limit interpretation of the competition experiments, the common effect of amino acid substitution on VLRB and Ig binding argues strongly for convergent recognition of highly overlapping epitopes.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar binding patterns to drifted viruses shown in Table 1.

claim: The overall immunodominance profile of IAV immunogens in mammals and lamprey responding to inactivated intact virus is similar.
source: Equally surprising is the similarity of the overall immunodominance profile of IAV immunogens in mammals and lamprey responding to inactivated intact virus: the HA globular domain is favored over the stem; HA is favored over NA; and internal proteins, despite their relative abundance in the virion, are weakly (NP) or undetectably (M1) immunogenic.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The HA globular domain is favored over the stem in both mammals and lamprey.
source: Equally surprising is the similarity of the overall immunodominance profile of IAV immunogens in mammals and lamprey responding to inactivated intact virus: the HA globular domain is favored over the stem; HA is favored over NA; and internal proteins, despite their relative abundance in the virion, are weakly (NP) or undetectably (M1) immunogenic.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: HA is favored over NA in both mammals and lamprey.
source: Equally surprising is the similarity of the overall immunodominance profile of IAV immunogens in mammals and lamprey responding to inactivated intact virus: the HA globular domain is favored over the stem; HA is favored over NA; and internal proteins, despite their relative abundance in the virion, are weakly (NP) or undetectably (M1) immunogenic.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Internal proteins, despite their relative abundance in the virion, are weakly (NP) or undetectably (M1) immunogenic.
source: Equally surprising is the similarity of the overall immunodominance profile of IAV immunogens in mammals and lamprey responding to inactivated intact virus: the HA globular domain is favored over the stem; HA is favored over NA; and internal proteins, despite their relative abundance in the virion, are weakly (NP) or undetectably (M1) immunogenic.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements.

claim: Total plasma VLRB concentration increases after immunization.
source: We confirmed the Pancer group's finding that total plasma VLRB concentration increases after immunization (Alder et al., 2005).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and supported by citation.

claim: Total Ig can increase in jawed fish after immunization.
source: Total Ig can also increase in jawed fish after immunization (Castro et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In mammals, high levels of Ig are maintained constitutively.
source: This differs from mammals, where high levels are maintained constitutively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian immunology.

claim: Lampreys can respond to purified IAV without additional adjuvant.
source: The ability of lampreys to respond to purified IAV without additional adjuvant indicates that lampreys recognize viral RNA or other viral innate immune activating molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental immunization protocol described in the Materials and methods.

claim: Lampreys recognize viral RNA or other viral innate immune activating molecules.
source: The ability of lampreys to respond to purified IAV without additional adjuvant indicates that lampreys recognize viral RNA or other viral innate immune activating molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of lampreys to respond to purified virus without adjuvant.

claim: Individual lampreys mount VLRB responses against different antigenic sites.
source: We also show in competition assays that individual lampreys mount VLRB responses against different antigenic sites.
evidence: This is supported by experimental competition data shown in Table 2.

claim: The four available VLRB-antigen crystal structures reveal many similarities in Ig and VLRB antigen recognition.
source: It is surprising that such structurally disparate molecules as Ig and VLRB receptors recognize the same proteins with overlapping epitopes. These recognition systems have evolved independently for >500 Mya, presumably shaped by different selective pressures from the environment, self-tolerance, and microorganisms. These differences notwithstanding, the four available VLRB-antigen crystal structures reveal many similarities in Ig and VLRB antigen recognition.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published crystal structures.

claim: In the two VLRB structures with protein antigens, the contact area is approximately 1500 Å2, which is in the same range as reported for Igs (1400–2300 Å2).
source: In the two VLRB structures with protein antigens (hen egg lysozyme and anthrax coat protein, BclA), the contact area (∼1500 Å2) is in the same range as reported for Igs (1400–2300 Å2), and utilizes the same non-covalent forces (salt bridges, hydrogen bonds, and van der Waals contacts) in similar proportions to mediate binding, which requires close shape complementarity to the antigen (Velikovsky et al., 2009; Kirchdoerfer et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published crystal structures cited.

claim: VLRB and Ig utilize the same non-covalent forces (salt bridges, hydrogen bonds, and van der Waals contacts) in similar proportions to mediate binding.
source: In the two VLRB structures with protein antigens (hen egg lysozyme and anthrax coat protein, BclA), the contact area (∼1500 Å2) is in the same range as reported for Igs (1400–2300 Å2), and utilizes the same non-covalent forces (salt bridges, hydrogen bonds, and van der Waals contacts) in similar proportions to mediate binding, which requires close shape complementarity to the antigen (Velikovsky et al., 2009; Kirchdoerfer et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published crystal structures cited.

claim: In the VLRB-HEL structure, the relatively small, crescent-shaped VLRB binds to an epitope in the catalytic cleft.
source: In the VLRB-HEL structure, the relatively small, crescent-shaped VLRB binds to an epitope in the catalytic cleft, whereas larger, dimeric Ig VHVL Abs bind to flatter epitopes away from the catalytic site.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published crystal structures.

claim: Larger, dimeric Ig VHVL Abs bind to flatter epitopes away from the catalytic site of HEL.
source: In the VLRB-HEL structure, the relatively small, crescent-shaped VLRB binds to an epitope in the catalytic cleft, whereas larger, dimeric Ig VHVL Abs bind to flatter epitopes away from the catalytic site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ig-HEL interactions.

claim: Single-chain camelid VHH and shark IgNAR favor the catalytic cleft of HEL that is presumably sterically inaccessible to dimeric VHVL Abs.
source: Interestingly, structures of single-chain camelid VHH and shark IgNAR have revealed that they also favor the catalytic cleft of HEL that is presumably sterically inaccessible to dimeric VHVL Abs (Velikovsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural studies.

claim: Analysis of hundreds of VLRB sequences has revealed a bias towards aromatic amino acids at the variable positions on the concave surface.
source: Analysis of hundreds of VLRB sequences has previously revealed a bias towards aromatic amino acids at the variable positions on the concave surface (Velikovsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior sequence analysis.

claim: When only the antigen contacting residue frequency is quantified, the amino acids are biased towards Tyr, Trp, Asn, and Asp residues.
source: In these analyses, less than half of the variable position residues contact antigen. When only the antigen contacting residue frequency is quantified, the amino acids are biased towards Tyr, Trp, Asn, and Asp residues (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 5.

claim: A similar bias towards Tyr, Trp, Asn, and Asp residues in antigen-contacting positions of Ig has been observed.
source: A similar bias towards these residues in antigen-contacting positions of Ig has also been observed (Mian et al., 1991; Davies and Cohen, 1996; Ramaraj et al., 2012; Robin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on Ig structure.

claim: The similarities in amino acid bias may account for the recognition of similar epitopes by Ig and VLRB.
source: These similarities may account for the recognition of similar epitopes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed similarities.

claim: The amino acid bias in Ig and VLRB may represent the optimal general solution for producing a single family of receptors capable of recognizing an infinite array of antigens with high specificity and affinity.
source: If so, this may also represent the optimal general solution for producing a single family of receptors capable of recognizing what is essentially an infinite array of antigens with high specificity and affinity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary significance of the observed similarities.

claim: The universality of Ig and VLRB antigenicity and immunogenicity provides strong support for the utility of animal models for understanding human Ab responses to vaccines and other medically relevant immunogens.
source: The universality of Ig and VLRB antigenicity and immunogenicity illuminated by our findings provides strong support for the utility of animal models for understanding human Ab responses to vaccines and other medically relevant immunogens.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: IAV is composed of four major structural proteins: hemagglutinin (HA), neuraminidase (NA), matrix protein (M1), and nucleoprotein (NP).
source: IAV is composed of four major structural proteins: two surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), embedded in a lipid envelope, lined by the matrix protein (M1), which encases the nucleoprotein (NP) coated viral genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus structure.

claim: Most HA-specific Igs with virus neutralizing activity bind to or bridge 5 antigenic regions in the globular domain (termed Sa, Sb, Ca1, Ca2, and Cb).
source: Most HA-specific Igs with virus neutralizing activity bind to or bridge 5 antigenic regions in the globular domain (termed Sa, Sb, Ca1, Ca2, and Cb), which surround the sialic acid receptor site that attaches HA to host cells (Gerhard et al., 1981).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior influenza research, supported by citation.

claim: Variation in the five antigenic sites as IAV evolves in the human population ('antigenic drift') prevents effective IAV vaccination.
source: Variation in these sites as IAV evolves in the human population ('antigenic drift') prevents effective IAV vaccination, necessitating frequent changes in vaccine formulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza virus evolution and vaccination challenges.

claim: Humans can generate protective Igs to conserved structures in the membrane-proximal HA stem.
source: The recent discovery that humans can generate protective Igs to conserved structures in the membrane-proximal HA stem have raised hopes of more effective vaccination if stem responses can be augmented using appropriately designed vaccines (Laursen and Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Jawless and jawed vertebrates last shared a common ancestor approximately 550 million years ago.
source: Jawless and jawed vertebrates last shared a common ancestor ∼550 Mya.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is established evolutionary knowledge.

claim: VLR genes are only in jawless vertebrates, whereas Immunoglobulin (Ig) genes are only in jawed vertebrates.
source: VLR genes are only in jawless vertebrates, whereas Immunoglobulin (Ig) genes are only in jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is established knowledge.

claim: Both jawed and jawless vertebrates have a lymphocyte-based adaptive immune system.
source: However, both jawed and jawless vertebrates have a lymphocyte-based adaptive immune system suggesting that the genetic programs necessary for lymphocyte development originated in a common ancestor before the antigen receptor genes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is established knowledge.

claim: The genetic programs necessary for lymphocyte development originated in a common ancestor before the antigen receptor genes.
source: However, both jawed and jawless vertebrates have a lymphocyte-based adaptive immune system suggesting that the genetic programs necessary for lymphocyte development originated in a common ancestor before the antigen receptor genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of lymphocyte-based immunity in both lineages, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cytidine deaminases are expressed by lymphocytes in both jawed and jawless vertebrates.
source: Cytidine deaminases are expressed by lymphocytes in both jawed and jawless vertebrates and may have originated in a common ancestor; activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) and cytosine deaminase (CDA).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is established knowledge.

claim: Cytidine deaminases may have originated in a common ancestor of jawed and jawless vertebrates.
source: Cytidine deaminases are expressed by lymphocytes in both jawed and jawless vertebrates and may have originated in a common ancestor; activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) and cytosine deaminase (CDA).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the presence of these enzymes in both lineages, as shown in Figure 1.
